Q: Why is xchg instruction with memory operand always atomic? A:

In my opinion, the reason is a compatibility tradeoff between 8086 and 80286 CPUs, but I found no Intel source that states the design rationale, so the explanation below is my speculation.

The 8086 CPU, released in 1978, actually had the design the question on why asks for for: XCHG with memory locked the bus only under an explicit LOCK prefix [1] [2], and the manual recommended LOCK XCHG as the semaphore idiom [1]. The implicit lock arrived with the 80286 (released in 1982), whose compatibility notes state it as a difference item: "The 80286 always asserts LOCK during an XCHG instruction with memory (even if the LOCK prefix was not used)" [3] [6]. The 286 datasheet states the hardware side of the same rule: the LOCK pin "may be activated explicitly by the LOCK instruction prefix or automatically by 80286 hardware during memory XCHG instructions, interrupt acknowledge, or descriptor table access" [5], which places the memory exchange in the same hardware-automatic locking class as interrupt acknowledge and descriptor-table access, operations whose locking the processor does not leave to software. The same 286 made the bare LOCK prefix IOPL-sensitive in protected mode [3] [4]. My understanding is that these changes fit together: since a bus lock stalls every bus master, the 286 restricted the prefix, yet semaphores live in exactly the user code that could lose access to it, so the implicit lock kept one bounded atomic primitive available at any privilege level ("regardless of the presence or absence of the LOCK prefix or of the value of the IOPL", as later manuals put it [8] [9]). This guarantee did not keep an existing LOCK XCHG instruction working unchanged when CPL was greater than IOPL, since the explicit prefix would still fault, and correct 8086 semaphore code already included that prefix. It instead made it possible to port such code by omitting the now-unnecessary prefix. What it cost was the unlocked register/memory swap, which in my opinion was worth little by 1982 (compilers emit laods and stores rather than swaps, and three MOVs and a scratch register do it non-atomically), and once software could rely on the guarantee, backward compatibility meant no later part could take it back [7].

So, to recapitulate what is written above, the atomicity is in the definition rather than in the prefix. With a memory operand, the processor applies its locking protocol for the whole exchange whether or not LOCK is written [8] [9], so a bare xchg is already an atomic swap. It is more exact to say that the locking protocol is implicit: an actual F0 LOCK-prefix byte need not be present, whereus ordinary arithmetic and bit-test read-modify-write instructions require an explicit prefix.

This atomcity costs what a locked read-modify-write costs. In the linked AIDA64 results, XCHG r,[m] and LOCK ADD [m],r have the same measured latency: 17.8 cycles on one Haswell desktop and 16.8 cycles on one Kaby Lake desktop, with throughput around 21.5 cycles in both cases [10]. Those numbers are best-case instruction-latency measurements, not a general cost under contention or when the cache line is elsewhere, and the table does not support saying that both CPUs are "roughly five times" slower than a plain store.

My FastMM4-AVX fork uses xchg to acquire its byte locks and a plain mov to release them. The current source actually writes lock xchg, so it does not rely on the prefix being omitted; the explicit prefix is merely redundant for a memory xchg, unless you are on a CPU older than 80286 ;-) Both accesses still have to be atomic, and the byte mov is atomic, but only the acquire needs an atomic read-modify-write and acquire ordering. On the hardware side, the plain store has release ordering on x86 because stores become visible in FIFO order [11]. This plain store is also how the current Linux x86 queued spinlock is released: smp_store_release, which x86 implements as a compiler barrier plus WRITE_ONCE, i.e. a plain store [12] [13].

In my opinion the plain release is the right performance tradeoff, but its behaviour should be described precisely. A locked release does nohting that explicitly "pushes" a cache line into a spinning core; cache coherence supplies the new value when that core can observe the line. It does, however, wait for older buffered stores and makes the locked operation globally visible before it completes, while a plain store lets the releasing core continue and may be observed later as its FIFO store buffer drains [11]. That delay is not architecturally bounded to a number of cycles merely because the buffer has finite capacity. A locked operation is also a full barrier, including StoreLoad ordering, whereas a plain release store supplies the ordering this spinlock needs without that extra constraint. So when the release doesn't have to be immedate from the releasing core's point of view, the cheaper non-locking release is what I like ;-)

Sources

  1. Intel, The 8086 Family User's Manual (1979), section 2.5 and the XCHG entry: another processor can access the semaphore between the read and write unless XCHG is preceded by LOCK
  2. Andrew Jenner, 8086 microcode disassembled, extracted from Ken Shirriff's die photographs: XCHG rm,r is five microinstructions with no lock micro-operation, and the LOCK prefix is handled outside the microcode
  3. Intel, 80286 and 80287 Programmer's Reference Manual, including the LOCK entry with its #GP(0) exception when CPL is greater than IOPL, protected-mode privilege rules, and Appendix C's 8086/8088 compatibility list
  4. 80286 manual, LOCK entry, stating that LOCK may be used only when CPL is no greater than IOPL
  5. AMD, 80286 High Performance Microprocessor datasheet (1985), LOCK pin description on page 5; the second-source datasheet carries the same pin description as Intel's
  6. MS-DOS Encyclopedia, Appendix M, 8086/8088 software compatibility issues, reproducing the 80286 difference item that memory XCHG always asserts LOCK
  7. 80386 Programmer's Reference Manual, section 14.8, whose first 80286 difference item is that the 80286 implements the bus lock function differently than the 80386, while the implicit XCHG lock itself carries forward unchanged
  8. 80386 Programmer's Reference Manual, XCHG, with the "regardless of the presence or absence of the LOCK prefix or of the value of the IOPL" wording and the semaphore sentence
  9. Intel SDM Volume 2B, XCHG excerpt, carrying the same architectural rule for later processors
  10. AIDA64 measurements collected in this Stack Overflow answer, including the Haswell and Kaby Lake latency and throughput tables
  11. Sewell et al., x86-TSO: A Rigorous and Usable Programmer's Model for x86 Multiprocessors, especially sections 3 and 4 on FIFO store buffers, locked instructions, and a Linux spinlock released by MOV
  12. Current Linux generic queued-spinlock implementation, whose unlock operation is smp_store_release(&lock->locked, 0)
  13. Current Linux x86 barrier definitions, implementing smp_store_release with a compiler barrier and WRITE_ONCE
  14. Stephen Morse et al., Intel Microprocessors: 8008 to 8086, checked for background only: it was published before the 80286 and therefore cannot document the rationale for the later change
